docs.title: LisPython
docs.text: This documentation stands for version 0.6.0 Try LisPy without installing it! : Web REPL

docs.title: What is LisPython?
docs.text:
Lisp + Python = LisPython. I'll use the abbreviation LisPy throughout this documentation. LisPy provides a new lisp-like syntax for Python. (Thus, macro system too)

LisPy is highly inspired by Clojure and Hy. I started this project because I want something slightly different from Hy. As a standalone language, Hy evolves fast. It can be good in general. But it's hard for me to keep track of the breaking changes in Hy.

docs.title: Macros
docs.text: LisPy's macro system is highly inspired by Clojure's macro system. You can check out the Chapter 7 and Chapter 8 of "Brave Clojure" for more information about Clojure's macro system.

docs.title: Macro Definition
docs.text:
Just change def in function definition to defmacro. And macros usually return a quoted expression. 

(defmacro name [args*]
  body*)

docs.title: Macro Example
docs.text:
(defmacro unless [test *body]
  (return `(if (not ~test)
             (do ~@body))))

(unless done
  (print "working"))
Python version 
if not done:
    print("working")
The built-in macros (below) are written the same way; their definitions are in src/lispy/macros/sugar.lpy.

docs.title: require
docs.text:
Loads the macros of a module so the file can use them. Macros are compile-time only: require leaves no runtime import behind.

LisPy version 

(require mod)          ; every macro, as mod.name
(require mod *)        ; every macro, unqualified
(require mod [a b])    ; only a and b, unqualified
(require mod [])       ; none
- (require mod) registers each macro of mod under the qualified name mod.name, so it is called as (mod.name ...). - (require mod *) registers every macro under its own name. - (require mod [a b]) registers just the listed macros under their own names. - (require mod []) registers nothing.

A module that cannot be found is a warning (could not load macros from 'mod' (module not found)), not an error; a macro that was never registered then fails where it is used.

docs.title: Built-in macros
docs.text:
The built-in macros are loaded in every module and in the REPL with no require. A module's own defmacros and explicit requires add to them, and (require mod *) never re-exports the built-ins.

To load only some of them, make (require lispy.macros <selection>) the module's first form (after an optional docstring); the selection replaces the built-ins: 

(require lispy.macros [-> when])   ; only -> and when
(require lispy.macros [])          ; none
(require lispy.macros *)           ; all (the default)
A bare (require lispy.macros) leaves only the qualified (lispy.macros.inc ...) names. A later require of lispy.macros only adds macros.

Binding a name that is an active macro (def, class, =, parameters, a defmacro's parameters and locals, loop and with targets, imports, match captures, ...) is a compile error, because (inc ...) would still expand the macro. Rename the binding, or opt out of that macro with a selection that omits it. A hyphenated macro name is compared as a Python name, so a binding my_x clashes with a macro my-x; a macro spelled otherwise (->, --, ok?) clashes only with a binding of that same spelling, not with the name it mangles to (_to_, __, ok_p).

The Python version in each example is what l2py prints.

docs.title: cond
docs.text:
(cond test then test then ... else)

Nested if statements: each test/then pair is one branch (elif after the first) and a trailing odd operand is the final else. It is a statement and yields no value: use conde for a value, and (do ...) for a branch of several forms.

LisPy version 

(cond (< x 0) (print "neg")
      (== x 0) (print "zero")
      (print "pos"))
Python version 
if x < 0:
    print("neg")
elif x == 0:
    print("zero")
else:
    print("pos")

docs.title: conde
docs.text:
(conde test then test then ... else)

The expression form of cond: a chain of ife whose trailing odd operand is the final else. Always give the else: with an even number of operands the last test is never evaluated and its then is the else.

LisPy version 

(= label (conde (< x 0) "neg"
                (== x 0) "zero"
                "pos"))
Python version 
label = "neg" if x < 0 else "zero" if x == 0 else "pos"

docs.title: ->
docs.text:
(-> value form ...)

Thread-first: insert value as the first argument of the first form, that result as the first argument of the next, and so on. A form that is not a parenthesised call, such as a bare name, is called with the value: (-> x f (g 2)) is g(f(x), 2).

LisPy version 

(-> x (f 1) (g 2))
Python version 
g(f(x, 1), 2)

docs.title: ->>
docs.text:
(->> value form ...)

Thread-last: insert value as the last argument of the first form, that result as the last argument of the next, and so on. A form that is not a parenthesised call, such as a bare name, is called with the value, but the steps after it then thread first instead of last: write every step as a parenthesised call.

LisPy version 

(->> x (f 1) (g 2))
Python version 
g(2, f(1, x))

docs.title: as->
docs.text:
(as-> value name form ...)

Bind name to value, then to each form's result in turn, and yield the last result, so name can stand anywhere in a form. An expression: each form is evaluated once, left to right, in the caller's scope.

Unlike -> (thread first) and ->> (thread last), as-> lets you name the threaded value and place it anywhere in each form: 

(as-> 0 x
  (+ x 10)     ;; x = 10
  (* 2 x)      ;; x = 20
  (str x))     ;; x = "20"

This expands to a single expression, a tuple of walrus assignments indexed with -1: 

((__x_0 := 0), (__x_0 := (__x_0 + 10)), (__x_0 := (2 * __x_0)), str(__x_0))[-1]

Because it is an expression, as-> works anywhere: as a return value, a call argument, a lambda body, or nested. CPython refuses := in some positions (e.g. a comprehension's iterable, annotations, type-alias values); there it is a loud compile error, so bind the value first.

The name is replaced only where it is read as a variable, not in keyword-argument names, quoted data, or the body of a fn/lambda that rebinds it.

Useful when the threaded value doesn't always go in the first or last position.

docs.title: fn
docs.text:
(fn [args] body)

Alias of lambda: an anonymous function whose body is one expression.

LisPy version

Python version

docs.title: comment
docs.text:
(comment body...)

Ignore the body: nothing in it is compiled or evaluated, and the form expands to None.

LisPy version

(print "done")
Python version 
None
print("done")

docs.title: when
docs.text:
(when test body...)

An if statement with no else, whose branch runs every body form in order. A statement: it yields no value.

LisPy version 

(when (> x 0)
  (print "positive")
  (= y x))
Python version 
if x > 0:
    print("positive")
    y = x

docs.title: gensym
docs.text:
gensym generates unique symbols to avoid variable name collisions in macros. It is automatically available inside defmacro bodies.

(gensym)          ;; => Symbol("__gensym_0")
(gensym "tmp")    ;; => Symbol("__tmp_1")
(gensym 'tmp)     ;; => Symbol("__tmp_2")  (also accepts a quoted Symbol)

The prefix can be a string or a symbol. Each call increments a global counter, so every generated symbol is unique.

docs.title: Why gensym?
docs.text:
Without gensym, a macro that introduces a local variable can accidentally shadow a variable in the caller's scope: 

;; BAD: if the caller has a variable named `tmp`, this breaks
(defmacro broken-swap [a b]
  (return `(do (= tmp ~a)
               (= ~a ~b)
               (= ~b tmp))))

Using gensym prevents this: 

(defmacro swap [a b]
  (= tmp (gensym "tmp"))
  (return `(do (= ~tmp ~a)
               (= ~a ~b)
               (= ~b ~tmp))))

Now (swap x y) expands to something like: 

__tmp_0 = x
x = y
y = __tmp_0
The generated name __tmp_0 won't collide with user variables.

docs.title: Just a new syntax for Python
docs.text: LisPy is not a new language. It is just a new syntax for Python. You can just think in Python, write in LisPy. You'll experience less breaking changes. It also provides some pythonic syntax such as "list comprehensions".

docs.title: Python Interop: 100% Compatible with Vanila Python
docs.text: LisPy is 100% compatible with Python. You can use any Python libraries and modules in LisPy. You can also use LisPy modules in Python.

docs.title: Import numpy in LisPy
docs.text: (import numpy as np)

docs.title: Import LisPy Code in Python
docs.text:
When you have function bar in foo.lpy file 

import lispy # it makes python interop available
from foo import bar
foo()

docs.title: Macro system
docs.text:
LisPy has a Lisp-like macro system. This can be achieved by its s-expression-like syntax.

I recommend reading Paul Graham’s article Beating the Average, which illustrates why macro systems are valuable.

docs.title: Macro example
docs.text:
do-while macro 

; do-while macro example
(defmacro do-while [pred *body]
  (return `(do
             ~@body
             (while ~pred
               ~@body))))

(do-while False (print "Does it really happen?"))
Translated into Python: 
print('Does it really happen?')
while False:
    print('Does it really happen?')

docs.title: Formatted String Literals
docs.text:
LisPy version 

(= name "World")
f"Hello, {(* 2 name)}!"
Python version 
name = "World"
f"Hello, {2 * name}!"
Replacement fields follow Python's rules: {{/}} are literal braces, !r/!s/!a conversions, format specs with nested fields, and {x=}. A field is ordinary code, so a string in it is written with plain quotes as in Python 3.12+ (f"{(.get d "k")}"), on every supported Python. The old spelling with \" (f"{(.get d \"k\")}") is deprecated: it still compiles, with a SyntaxWarning (shown by default, as for an invalid escape sequence in Python 3.12+), and a string opened with \" must be closed by \". LisPy version 
f"{{literal}} {x!r:>{width}} {x=}"
Python version 
f"{{literal}} {x!r:>{width}} {x=}"

docs.title: Template String Literals
docs.text:
Python 3.14+ (PEP 750). The t prefix combines with r like f does (rt"...", Tr"...") and builds a string.templatelib.Template. Each interpolation's expression is the LisPy text inside the braces. On an older Python a t-string is a compile error naming the version it needs.

LisPy version 

(= name "World")
t"Hello, {(* 2 name)!r:>12}!"
Python version 
name = "World"
t"Hello, {2 * name!r:>12}!"  # interpolations[0].expression == "(* 2 name)"

docs.title: Attribute
docs.text: Two forms read an attribute: a dotted name, and (. obj attr).

docs.title: Dotted Name
docs.text:
A name with dots in it is Python's attribute access. It chains, and it works anywhere a name does: as a value, a call head, an assignment or del target, and in import.

LisPy version 

a.b.c
(obj.method arg :kwarg value)
(= obj.attr 1)
(+= obj.count 1)
(del obj.attr)
(import os.path)
Python version 
a.b.c
obj.method(arg, kwarg=value)
obj.attr = 1
obj.count += 1
del obj.attr
import os.path
Every part is an ordinary name, so hyphens become underscores (a.b-c is a.b_c). The dotted name must be one token that starts with a name: a. and a..b are errors, a lone .a as a value is an error ((.a obj) is the method-call form below), and a.b[0] is refused (use (sub a.b 0)).

docs.title: (. obj attr)
docs.text:
The object may be any expression, which a dotted name cannot be: a literal, call, subscription or other form on the left of the dot is not read as attribute access ((f).x and "s".upper are errors). (. obj attr) takes the attribute names after the object, so more than one chains them.

LisPy version 

(. obj attr)
(. obj a b)
(. (f) attr)
(. (sub items 0) attr)
(. "text" upper)
Python version 
obj.attr
obj.a.b
f().attr
items[0].attr
"text".upper
Each attribute must be a plain name, so (. obj (method)) is an error: to call a method on an expression use the method-call form below.

Python version 
obj.method_name(arg1, arg2, *args, kwarg1=value1, kwarg2=value2, **kwargs)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
In this section, I'll give a pair of LisPy code and corresponding Python code for each AST node. Checkout the Python AST documentation for more information about each node.

Corresponding python code is generated by l2py command in usage section.

Python version

docs.title: Lexical syntax
docs.text:
• ; starts a comment that runs to the end of the line. It ends any token, so a comment may follow with no space: (print "a"); comment.
  • Hyphens in a name become underscores in Python: my-var is my_var.
  • :kw value inside a call is the keyword argument kw=value: (f a :kw 1 :other-kw 2) is f(a, kw=1, other_kw=2).
  • *x and **x unpack a sequence or mapping in a call: (f *xs **kw) is f(*xs, **kw). The * or ** is glued to the form.
  • ^type is a type annotation; it follows the name it annotates: (def f [a ^int b] ^int ...) is def f(a: int, b) -> int, and (= a ^int 1) is a: int = 1.
  • ', `, ~ and ~@ (quote, syntax-quote, unquote, unquote-splicing) are glued to the form they apply to; ' x is an error.
  • A string may span lines: the line break is part of the string.

docs.title: Form Reference
docs.text: Every LisPython form with its usage and a one-line description: the same text the editor shows on hover. Each form links to its examples on the Statements, Expressions and Macros pages.

docs.title: Statements
docs.text: Form Usage Description def (def name [args] body...) Define a function. Arguments are given in a bracket list. An optional docstring can follow the argument list. async-def (async-def name [args] body...) Define an async function (coroutine). deco (deco decorator definition) or (deco [decorator ...] definition) Apply a decorator to the following function/class definition. return (return value) Return a value from a function. class (class name [bases] body...) Define a class. Bases are given in a bracket list. type (type Name value)(type Name[T] value) Define a type alias (Python 3.12+). del (del target...) Delete a name or item. = (= target... value) or (= target ^annotation value), value optional after an annotation Assignment statement. += (+= target value...) Augmented assignment (target += value). -= (-= target value...) Augmented assignment (target -= value). *= (*= target value...) Augmented assignment (target *= value). /= (/= target value...) Augmented assignment (target /= value). //= (//= target value...) Augmented assignment (target //= value). %= (%= target value...) Augmented assignment (target %= value). **= (**= target value...) Augmented assignment (target **= value). <<= (<<= target value...) Augmented assignment (target <<= value). >>= (>>= target value...) Augmented assignment (target >>= value). |= (|= target value...) Augmented assignment (target |= value). ^= (^= target value...) Augmented assignment (target ^= value). &= (&= target value...) Augmented assignment (target &= value). @= (@= target value...) Augmented assignment (target @= value). for (for target in iterable body...) For loop. target is bound to each element of iterable. async-for (async-for target in iterable body...) Async for loop — use inside async-def. while (while test body...) While loop. if (if test then else...) Conditional statement. Compiles to Python if/else. do (do body...) A statement block grouping several statements where one statement is expected (e.g. an if branch); not an expression. with (with [context as target ...] body...), each as target optional Context manager statement. async-with (async-with [context as target ...] body...), each as target optional Async context manager — use inside async-def. case (case pattern as name if guard body...), as name and if guard optional One arm of a match: a pattern, an optional as name and if guard, then the body. raise (raise), (raise exception) or (raise exception from cause) Raise an exception. try (try body... (except ...)... (else ...) (finally ...)) Try/except/finally statement. except (except [type ... as name] body...) or (except body...), as name optional Exception handler clause of a try. else (else body...) Clause of a try that runs when no exception was raised. finally (finally body...) Clause of a try that always runs on exit. except* (except* [type ... as name] body...), as name optional Exception-group handler clause of a try (Python 3.11+). assert (assert test) or (assert test message) Assert that a condition is true. import (import module)(import module as alias) Import a module. from (from module [names...])(from module [name as alias ...]) Import specific names from a module. lazy-import (lazy-import module)(lazy-import module as alias) Import a module lazily: it is loaded on first use (Python 3.15+). lazy-from (lazy-from module [names...])(lazy-from module [name as alias ...]) Import names from a module lazily: it is loaded on first use (Python 3.15+). global (global name...) Declare names as global variables. nonlocal (nonlocal name...) Declare names as nonlocal variables. pass (pass) No-op placeholder statement. break (break) Break out of a loop. continue (continue) Continue to the next loop iteration.

docs.title: Expressions
docs.text: Form Usage Description match (match subject (case ...)...) Structural pattern matching (Python 3.10+). and (and value...) Logical AND (short-circuit). or (or value...) Logical OR (short-circuit). | (| a b ...)(| pattern pattern...) Bitwise OR as an operator; inside a case, an or-pattern matching any alternative. + Arithmetic addition / unary positive. - Arithmetic subtraction / unary negative. * Arithmetic multiplication / iterable unpacking. / True division. // Floor (integer) division. % Modulo (remainder). ** Exponentiation. @ Matrix multiplication. << Bitwise left shift. >> Bitwise right shift. ^ Bitwise XOR. & Bitwise AND. not Logical NOT. ~ Bitwise NOT / unquote (inside quasiquote). == (== a b...) Equality test. > (> a b...) Greater than. != (!= a b...) Inequality test. < (< a b...) Less than. <= (<= a b...) Less than or equal. >= (>= a b...) Greater than or equal. is (is a b...) Identity test (x is y). is-not (is-not a b...) Negated identity test (x is not y). in (in a b...) Membership test (x in y). not-in (not-in a b...) Negated membership test (x not in y). := (:= name value) Walrus operator (assignment expression). lambda (lambda [args] body) Anonymous function (lambda expression). ife (ife test then else), else optional Ternary conditional expression (then if test else else). , (, a b c) Tuple literal. await (await value) Await a coroutine. yield (yield) or (yield value) Yield a value from a generator. yield-from (yield-from iterable) Yield all values from a sub-generator. f-string f"text {expr} more" Formatted string literal (f-string). . (. value attr...) Attribute access (obj.attr); (. obj a b) is obj.a.b. sub (sub value index...) Subscript access (obj[index]); more indexes subscript again.

docs.title: Macro system
docs.text: Form Usage Description ' Quote — prevent evaluation; return the form as data. ` Quasiquote — like quote but allows unquote (~) splicing. ~@ Unquote-splice — splice a list into a quasiquote. defmacro (defmacro name [args] body...) Define a compile-time macro. The macro receives unevaluated S-expressions and must return an S-expression. require (require module)(require module *)(require module [names...]) Import macros from a LisPython macro module at compile time. (require module) registers every macro as module.name, * registers every macro unqualified, and a list registers exactly those names — an empty [] registers none.

docs.title: Built-in macros
docs.text:
A .lpy file needs (require lispy.macros *) before it can use the built-in macros (cond, ->, fn, ...); the REPL and nREPL load them already.

Form Usage Description cond (cond test then test then ... else) Nested if statements: each test/then pair is one branch (elif after the first) and a trailing odd operand is the final else. It is a statement and yields no value: use conde for a value, and (do ...) for a branch of several forms. conde (conde test then test then ... else) The expression form of cond: a chain of ife whose trailing odd operand is the final else. Always give the else: with an even number of operands the last test is never evaluated and its then is the else. -> (-> value form ...) Thread-first: insert value as the first argument of the first form, that result as the first argument of the next, and so on. A form that is not a parenthesised call, such as a bare name, is called with the value: (-> x f (g 2)) is g(f(x), 2). ->> (->> value form ...) Thread-last: insert value as the last argument of the first form, that result as the last argument of the next, and so on. A form that is not a parenthesised call, such as a bare name, is called with the value, but the steps after it then thread first instead of last: write every step as a parenthesised call. as-> (as-> value name form ...) Bind name to value, then to each form's result in turn, and yield the last result, so name can stand anywhere in a form. An expression: each form is evaluated once, left to right, in the caller's scope. fn (fn [args] body) Alias of lambda: an anonymous function whose body is one expression. comment (comment body...) Ignore the body: nothing in it is compiled or evaluated, and the form expands to None. when (when test body...) An if statement with no else, whose branch runs every body form in order. A statement: it yields no value. inc (inc value) The expression value + 1; value itself is left unchanged. dec (dec value) The expression value - 1; value itself is left unchanged. ++ (++ target) The statement target += 1. -- (-- target) The statement target -= 1.

docs.title: Function Definitions
docs.text:
LisPy version 

(deco [decorator1
       decorator2]
  (def function-name [arg1 arg2 *args :kwarg1 value1 :kwarg2 value2 **kwargs]
    "docstring"
    body1
    body2
    (return value)))
Python version 
@decorator1
@decorator2
def function_name(arg1, arg2, *args, kwarg1=value1, kwarg2=value2, **kwargs):
    """docstring"""
    body1
    body2
    return value

docs.title: Async Function Definitions
docs.text: Use async-def instead of def.

docs.title: deco
docs.text:
Decorates the definition (def, async-def or class) it wraps: (deco decorator definition) for one decorator, (deco [d1 d2] definition) for several, listed top to bottom and applied bottom-up as in Python: the last one wraps the definition first, so (deco [d1 d2] ...) is d1(d2(f)). A decorator is any expression, a call included.

LisPy version 

(deco my-decorator
  (def f [x] (return x)))

(deco [d1 (d2 1)]
  (def g [x] (return x)))

(deco register
  (class A []
    (pass)))
Python version 
@my_decorator
def f(x):
    return x


@d1
@d2(1)
def g(x):
    return x


@register
class A:
    pass

docs.title: return
docs.text:
(return) returns None; (return value) returns the value. It takes at most one value: return several as a tuple with (, a b).

LisPy version 

(def f [x]
  (return x))
(def g []
  (return))
(def h [x y]
  (return (, x y)))
Python version 
def f(x):
    return x


def g():
    return


def h(x, y):
    return (x, y)

docs.title: Class Definition
docs.text:
LisPy version 

(deco [decorator1
       decorator2]
  (class class-name [base-class1 base-class2]
    "docstring"
    body))
Python version 
@decorator1
@decorator2
class class_name(base_class1, base_class2):
    """docstring"""

    body

docs.title: Generic Functions and Classes
docs.text:
Python 3.12+ (PEP 695); defaults need Python 3.13+ (PEP 696). Write the type parameters glued to the name, with no space: f[T] is a generic name, while f [T] is a name followed by a list. The bracket uses the argument markers of def: ^ for a bound (a tuple bound is a constraint list), * for a TypeVarTuple, ** for a ParamSpec and : for a default. On an older Python these forms are a compile error naming the version they need.

A glued name is only valid as the name of def, async-def, class and type; to subscript, use (sub xs ...).

LisPy version 

(def first[T] [xs ^(sub list T)] ^T
  (return (sub xs 0)))

(class Box[T ^(, int str) *Ts **P] [Base]
  (pass))

(def f[:T str :U ^int bool :*Ts *(sub tuple int) :**P [int str]] []  ; Python 3.13+
  (pass))
Python version 
def first[T](xs: list[T]) -> T:
    return xs[0]

class Box[T: (int, str), *Ts, **P](Base):
    pass

def f[T = str, U: int = bool, *Ts = *tuple[int], **P = [int, str]]():  # Python 3.13+
    pass

docs.title: Type Alias
docs.text:
Python 3.12+ (PEP 695). As in Python, type is a soft keyword: (type NAME value) and (type NAME[T ...] value) are a type alias only as a statement with exactly two operands whose first is a plain name. Every other shape is a call to the builtin type, so (= t (type x)) and (type "N" (, object) {}) are unchanged. If you rebind type and need a bare two-argument call as a statement, write (= _ (type a b)). On an older Python the alias is a compile error naming the version it needs.

LisPy version 

(type Number (| int float))
(type Vec[T] (sub list T))
Python version 
type Number = int | float
type Vec[T] = list[T]

docs.title: match
docs.text:
LisPy version 

(match x
  (case "Relevant"
        ...)
  (case None
        ...)
  (case [1 2]
        ...)
  (case [1 2 *rest]
        ...)
  (case [*_]
    ...)
  (case {1 _ 2 _}
    ...)
  (case {**rest}
    ...)
  (case (Point2D 0 0)
    ...)
  (case (Point3D :x 0 :y 0 :z 0)
    ...)
  (case [x] as y
    ...)
  (case _
    ...)
  (case (| [x] y)
    ...))
Python version 
match x:
    case "Relevant":
        ...
    case None:
        ...
    case [1, 2]:
        ...
    case [1, 2, *rest]:
        ...
    case [*_]:
        ...
    case {1: _, 2: _}:
        ...
    case {**rest}:
        ...
    case Point2D(0, 0):
        ...
    case Point3D(x=0, y=0, z=0):
        ...
    case [x] as y:
        ...
    case _:
        ...
    case [x] | y:
        ...

docs.title: Signed Literal Patterns
docs.text:
A negative number or a complex literal is a value pattern. A leading + needs Python 3.15+; on an older Python it is a compile error naming the version.

LisPy version 

(match x
  (case -1
    ...)
  (case -1-2j
    ...)
  (case {-1 _}
    ...)
  (case +1  ; Python 3.15+
    ...))
Python version 
match x:
    case -1:
        ...
    case -1 - 2j:
        ...
    case {-1: _}:
        ...
    case +1:  # Python 3.15+
        ...

docs.title: Lazy imports
docs.text:
Python 3.15+ (PEP 810). lazy-import and lazy-from take the same arguments as import and from; the module is loaded when a name is first used. As in Python, lazy-from refuses * and __future__, and a lazy import is not allowed inside a function, a class or a try block. On an older Python these forms are a compile error naming the version they need.

LisPy version 

(lazy-import json)
(lazy-import numpy as np)
(lazy-from json [dumps loads as load-json])
Python version 
lazy import json
lazy import numpy as np
lazy from json import dumps, loads as load_json

docs.title: REPL
docs.text:
lpy
#or
lpy -t #if you want to print python translation.

The REPL features Emacs-style keybindings (C-a, C-e, C-b, C-f, M-b, M-f, etc.), arrow key navigation, and persistent command history saved to ~/.lpy_history.

docs.title: Auto-closing pairs
docs.text:
The REPL automatically inserts closing brackets and quotes when you type an opening one:

You type REPL inserts Cursor position ( () between ( and ) [ [] between [ and ] { {} between { and } ' '' between the quotes " "" between the quotes
  • Typing a closing character (), ], }) when the cursor is already before one will skip over it instead of inserting a duplicate.
  • Typing a quote (', ") when the cursor is before the same quote will skip over it.
  • Pressing backspace between an empty pair deletes both characters.
